messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Adaeze is a 35-year-old Nigerian-American woman who works as a private tutor, primarily with elementary-aged children. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 55 following a rape that occurred approximately fourteen months ago. She was assaulted by an acquaintance in her own apartment on an evening she had initially described as unremarkable — she had been grading worksheets when he arrived uninvited. During the assault, a child in the neighbouring unit began crying loudly through the wall, and that sound continued, unanswered, for the duration of what happened to her. She has not been able to explain to anyone why that detail feels so central to what she carries now. She cannot fully put the experience into words at all — the memory resists language, surfacing instead as sensation, as the particular weight of helplessness, as a physical nausea that arrives without warning. When she does attempt to recall the event, the terror does not diminish with distance; it returns at full force, as though no time has passed. And yet the memory also feels strangely dissociated from her — as if it happened to another woman, someone she watches from a remove, which makes it simultaneously unreal and inescapable.

It is the memory's unprocessed, fragmented quality that makes her daily work so treacherous. Adaeze tutors children after school, and when one of her young students cries — over a frustrating math problem, over a scraped knee — the sound reaches her like a physical blow. In those moments, the incomplete memory surges forward, and with it comes a cascade of appraisals she has come to experience as simply true: that she is permanently changed, that something essential in her has been broken beyond repair, and that she cannot manage even this small upset without falling apart. The crying does not remind her of the assault so much as it briefly collapses the distance between then and now, and the certainty of her own damage arrives with the same force as the original terror.

Those appraisals — that she is ruined, that she cannot cope — have come to govern nearly every decision she makes. She has come to believe that if she allows herself to think carefully about what happened, she will not survive the thinking. This conviction has made her a dedicated avoider: she changes the subject when friends or her partner attempt to discuss what occurred, she declines social invitations that might carry the risk of genuine pleasure, and she has quietly stopped attending the community gatherings her mother hosts on Sunday afternoons. Her partner has noticed her withdrawal and named it, gently, more than once. She has not been able to explain it to him, partly because she cannot find the words, and partly because she is certain that if he understood how thoroughly she has changed, he would leave.

The avoidance, however, has not protected her. By refusing to engage with the memory, she has kept it raw and unintegrated, which means it continues to ambush her through the body — the nausea that rises when something is uncertain or unresolved, the way an unscheduled change to a tutoring session can send her into a spiral she cannot account for. Her rumination runs alongside the avoidance rather than replacing it: she returns, repeatedly, to what she should have done differently that evening, rehearsing her own culpability with a thoroughness that keeps the memory active without ever processing it. This self-blame, in turn, reinforces her conviction that she is permanently damaged — that the assault happened because of something in her, and that the damage is therefore her own to carry. The loop tightens: the more she blames herself, the more she avoids; the more she avoids, the more the memory remains fragmented and potent; the more potent the memory, the more unbearable the triggers become; and the more unbearable the triggers, the more certain she is that she cannot cope.

What finally brought Adaeze to seek help was a session last month in which a child began crying inconsolably and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she sat on the floor for twenty minutes, shaking. She told her partner she had a migraine. She is most afraid that therapy will require her to speak what she cannot yet put into words. What she is most hoping for — though she would not yet say this aloud — is that the woman she was before that evening might still, somehow, be recoverable.
